title: Understanding GitHub Pages Fixed URLs
reading_goal: I understand that the GitHub Pages URL is fixed and that only the content is updated after a push.
code:
# Example repository URL
https://github.com/<account>/<repository>

# Example project Pages URL
https://<account>.github.io/<repository>/
question: What happens to the URL after deploying a new commit while keeping the account, repository name, and Pages settings?
choices: A completely new address appears every time
The deployed content normally updates at the same address
answer: The deployed content normally updates at the same address
explanation: With the same account, repository, and Pages settings, a normal new deployment updates content at the same public URL. Renaming the repository or account or changing the custom domain or Pages source can change it. A project site includes the repository base path, so verify root-relative and relative asset paths at the actual deployed URL.
project_context: This card distinguishes a local development URL from a public GitHub Pages project URL.

title: Understanding the Loading Order of Static Apps
reading_goal: Understand the process by which the browser loads CSS and JavaScript from index.html.
question: How is app.js loaded in this HTML snippet?
choices: It is automatically generated within CSS
It loads from the Git commit message
It is loaded via the `src` attribute of the `script` tag
answer: It is loaded via the `src` attribute of the `script` tag
explanation: link requests the stylesheet, and the script src requests JavaScript. A defer script downloads in parallel with HTML parsing and executes in document order after parsing finishes but before DOMContentLoaded. A stylesheet can block rendering, and a deferred script may wait for a stylesheet needed for style calculation, so this does not guarantee that initial display is never delayed.
project_context: This is why we check whether the index page has opened and whether app.js has been requested when "Loading..." stops.

title: Reading About Static Resource Cache Busting
reading_goal: Understand the mechanism of bypassing the cache by appending a version query to CSS/JS URLs.
question: Why is “?v=20260529_force1” added?
choices: To permanently change the file name
I want to change the server port
To make the browser recognize it as a different URL from the previous file
I want to delete the HTML
answer: To make the browser recognize it as a different URL from the previous file
explanation: Changing the query changes the full URL, which ordinary browser and CDN caches may treat as a separate resource key. This can cause a new asset request, but it is not guaranteed if the server, CDN, or service worker ignores queries. A content hash or consistent version policy is easier to trace than arbitrary per-deployment text.
project_context: This is a versioned-asset URL pattern for reducing reuse of stale JavaScript and CSS after deployment.

title: Adding a version number to data fetches
reading_goal: Read the function that appends APP_DATA_VERSION to the JSON requests for "lesson" and "side card."
question: If the path in the data fetch URL already contains a "?", why do we add "&v="?
choices: Since the second query parameter and all subsequent ones must be separated by &,
answer: Since the second query parameter and all subsequent ones must be separated by &,
explanation: The first query parameter in an ordinary URL starts with ?, and later parameters use &, so the function appends &v= when a query already exists. String concatenation can place a parameter after a #fragment or duplicate an existing v. URL and URLSearchParams.set("v", APP_DATA_VERSION) preserve the URL structure and replace the value more safely.
project_context: This cache-refresh structure adds a data version to lesson JSON requests.

title: Interpreting the 304 Log
reading_goal: Understand that a 304 in the server logs is not an error but a cache-related response.
question: What is a 304 in index.html?
choices: A response indicating that the file was deleted
A response indicating that the server is down
Responses indicating that it is acceptable to use the browser cache
answer: Responses indicating that it is acceptable to use the browser cache
explanation: 304 Not Modified follows a conditional request containing a validator; the server says the resource has not changed and omits the body. The browser can use its cached body. This is not an error, but the status alone does not prove that the cached body is the intended deployment or that a service worker did not supply another response.
project_context: This is a practical exercise in distinguishing between 304 and 200 errors in local server validation logs.

title: Reading About Handling JSON Fetch Failures
reading_goal: Read the code that throws a clear error if the fetch response fails.
question: What happens if `res.ok` is false?
choices: It throws an error and does not proceed to JSON parsing
answer: It throws an error and does not proceed to JSON parsing
explanation: When res.ok is false, the function throws and does not run res.json. Even with a 2xx response, invalid JSON makes res.json reject, while a network error rejects fetch before a response exists. The caller should catch both categories, display safe path and error context, and avoid leaving the entire app on an endless Loading state.
project_context: This is necessary to identify the cause of the entire app's loading process stopping when a single JSON file returns a 404 error.

title: Reading the "Promise.all" Lesson
reading_goal: Understand the structure for loading multiple lesson files in parallel and the characteristics of failures.
question: What are the features of `Promise.all`?
choices: Commit the array to the auto-save
If even one of the requests fails, the entire process may fail.
Deletes files in no particular order
answer: If even one of the requests fails, the entire process may fail.
explanation: map creates each loadJson promise, and Promise.all resolves with results in input order only after every promise fulfills. One rejection rejects the overall await, but it does not automatically cancel other fetches that have started. Use fail-fast behavior for required files and Promise.allSettled or per-item fallback for optional ones according to policy.
project_context: This is why the app may get stuck on "Loading" if you add a file that isn't in `lessonFiles`.

title: Saving and Reading Progress in localStorage
reading_goal: Read the structure that saves learning progress in the browser.
code:
const progress = { seen: ["PY1_001"], unknown: [] };
localStorage.setItem("ptr_progress", JSON.stringify(progress));
question: Why use `JSON.stringify(progress)`?
choices: To compress an object into a file
To convert an object into a string that can be stored in localStorage,
answer: To convert an object into a string that can be stored in localStorage,
explanation: localStorage stores strings, so JSON.stringify serializes the object to a JSON string. The data remains in origin-specific browser storage and is readable by scripts on that origin, so it is unsuitable for secrets or sensitive personal data. The synchronous API can block the UI for large frequent writes, and setItem may fail because of quota, private mode, or storage policy.
project_context: This is how the "Study," "Don't Know," "Note," and "Today's Queue" statuses are saved in the browser.

title: Loading localStorage: Fallback Reading
reading_goal: Reads a structure that uses a default value when no value is stored.
code:
const raw = localStorage.getItem("ptr_progress");
const progress = raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : { seen: [], unknown: [] };
question: If there is no "raw," what is "progress"?
explanation: When raw is null, the conditional expression selects the default object, matching the answer. If raw exists but contains invalid JSON, JSON.parse throws; this code has no fallback for corruption. A safe loader catches parse errors, validates the parsed schema, records the problem, and deliberately selects a default.
project_context: This code ensures that even users opening the app for the first time start with an empty progress bar.

title: Reading the PWA manifest.json File
reading_goal: I understand that PWA installation information is contained in `manifest.json`.
question: Which of the following most closely matches the meaning of "display: standalone"?
choices: Always run it only on the server
Makes the browser run like an app with a less visible UI
answer: Makes the browser run like an app with a less visible UI
explanation: display="standalone" requests a standalone presentation with reduced browser UI when an installed app opens and the platform supports it. It does not by itself guarantee installability or presentation mode and may fall back by browser or platform. Verify name, icons, start_url, scope, and installation criteria such as HTTPS and service-worker support too.
project_context: It’s designed to be pinned to the phone’s home screen just like a learning app.

title: Understanding the Service Worker Cache Concept
reading_goal: I understand that a service worker can act as an intermediary between network requests and the cache.
question: What happens if there is a cache?
choices: It can return a cached response instead of accessing the network.
answer: It can return a cached response instead of accessing the network.
explanation: If caches.match finds a response, this cache-first flow returns it without going to the network. The snippet does not populate the cache or implement versioning, deletion, or a network-failure fallback. Cache-first is fast and useful offline but can serve stale assets for a long time, so install/activate version migration and update messaging are needed.
project_context: If the PWA cache is strong, you may still see the old code even after changing app.js.

title: DevTools Network Checkpoints
reading_goal: Learn how to use the browser's Network tab to see which files were actually loaded.
code:
Network tab check:
- index.html status
- app.js status and query version
- style.css status
- lesson JSON status
- side_cards JSON status
question: What should you inspect in Network when investigating a stuck Loading screen?
choices: The status, response, and version of app.js and JSON requests
answer: The status, response, and version of app.js and JSON requests
explanation: In Network, inspect the request URL, status, response body, initiator, and cache or service-worker indicators. A 200 does not prove that JavaScript ran or JSON parsed, and a 304 can be normal cache validation. Connect this evidence with Console errors and application state to locate the stalled stage.
project_context: By checking the server logs and the browser's Network tab at the same time, you can quickly narrow down the cause of cache, 404, and JavaScript errors.

title: Reading Errors in the DevTools Console
reading_goal: I understand that console errors provide the filename, line number, and message.
code:
Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '}'
    at app.js?v=20260529_force1:312:5
question: Where should I check first for this error?
explanation: The stack location makes line 312, column 5 of app.js the first place to inspect. A parser may detect a SyntaxError after the actual missing quote or brace, so the cause can be on an earlier line. For a generated or minified bundle, use source maps, and inspect the recent diff and syntax validation around the reported location.
project_context: It is important to check whether the parentheses are broken after replacing a function block.

title: Reading CSS for Mobile Screens
reading_goal: I'm reading about CSS that changes the layout when the screen width is narrow.
question: When is the `max-width: 720px` rule applied?
choices: When the server is on port 720
When the screen width is 720px or less
answer: When the screen width is 720px or less
explanation: A mobile layout is a way of arranging buttons and text so that they are clearly visible even on small screens. By using media queries, you can apply different CSS styles depending on the screen size. Therefore, the correct answer is “when the screen width is 720px or less.”
project_context: This is a way to reduce the problem of the right panel or code block becoming too wide on a phone.

title: Architecture for Connecting Static Apps to an API Server
reading_goal: Understand the structure in which a static PWA calls a separate API server using the `fetch` method.
code:
# static app
http://localhost:8790/src/pwa/index.html

# API server
http://127.0.0.1:8000/search?q=lidar

# browser JS
fetch("http://127.0.0.1:8000/search?q=" + encodeURIComponent(q))
question: What is the role of the 8790 server in this architecture?
choices: Direct Query of the Search Database
Serving static files such as HTML, CSS, and JS
answer: Serving static files such as HTML, CSS, and JS
explanation: In this example, the 8790 server provides frontend files such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, while the 8000 application creates search responses. The ports make them different origins, so CORS may be required. On a phone, 127.0.0.1 means the phone, not the PC, so use a public API host or the PC LAN address with correct bind and firewall settings.
project_context: This structure distinguishes origin and host when connecting a static learning frontend to a separate search API.

title: Read the Post-Deployment Verification Checklist
reading_goal: Learn the steps to verify that the app is actually displaying the latest files after a push.
code:
# 1. Confirm the commit and pushed target branch
# 2. Confirm CI/Pages success and source revision
# 3. Inspect public HTML, JS, and JSON status/response
# 4. Verify app.js and data content versions
# 5. Check Console errors and service-worker/cache state
question: If the latest changes aren't reflected after a push, what should you check in particular?
choices: It only checks the keyboard battery status
Just check the monitor resolution settings
Just check the GitHub username display
explanation: A clean local git status or one 200 response does not prove that the intended commit is publicly deployed. Compare the remote branch and deployment revision with response content and versions at the public URL, then inspect Console and service-worker cache state. Preserve evidence of which layer is stale before clearing caches so the cause remains traceable.
project_context: This is a routine for verifying a structure in which only the content is updated on a GitHub Pages permalink.
